fistula.hero.title: Anal Fistula Treatment
fistula.hero.lede: Repeated pus discharge, pain and swelling near the anus — an anal fistula usually does not heal on its own. The earlier it is assessed, the simpler the treatment is likely to be.
fistula.what.p1: An anal fistula is a small tunnel that forms between the inside of the anal canal and the skin near the anus. It most often develops after an infection near the anus that creates a collection of pus (an abscess); when the pus drains away, it can leave a channel behind.
fistula.what.p2: A fistula usually does not heal on its own — symptoms tend to keep returning, sometimes in a cycle of temporary closure followed by renewed infection. For this reason, surgery is advised in most cases, and the sooner it is assessed, the simpler the treatment is likely to be.
fistula.symptoms.i1: Constant, throbbing pain around the anus — often worse when sitting, moving, coughing or passing stool
fistula.symptoms.i3: Discharge of pus, blood or foul-smelling fluid near the anus; some people see a small hole in the skin
fistula.symptoms.i4: Swelling and redness around the anus, with a high temperature if an abscess is also present
fistula.symptoms.i5: The opening may seal over temporarily — pain and swelling then build up before it drains again
fistula.symptoms.i6: In some cases, difficulty controlling bowel movements
fistula.causes.p: Common causes and risk factors for an anal fistula:
fistula.causes.i1: Most fistulas develop after a perianal abscess — when the abscess does not heal completely after draining
fistula.causes.i2: Less common causes include inflammatory bowel disease such as Crohn's disease, and diverticulitis
fistula.causes.i3: Tuberculosis or HIV infection, previous surgery near the anus, pelvic radiation therapy, or injury to the area
fistula.causes.i4: Higher risk in men, in people who have had a perianal abscess before, in people with inflammatory bowel disease, and in people with weakened immune systems
fistula.causes.i5: About half of people with an infected anal gland may go on to develop a fistula (Cleveland Clinic)
fistula.when.p1: See a doctor for any persistent anal pain or discharge — do not assume it will settle by itself, and do not assume it is piles; piles are usually not this painful.
fistula.when.i1: Fever, swelling and redness around the anus, or rapidly increasing pain need urgent assessment — these can be signs of an abscess that needs draining
fistula.when.i2: Alongside the examination, proctoscopy/anoscopy and scans such as ultrasound or MRI may be used — the tunnel's pathway is mapped to plan the treatment
fistula.when.p2: If a general doctor suspects a fistula, they will usually refer you to a colorectal specialist, where the evaluation and planning take place.
fistula.treat.intro: Because a fistula usually does not heal on its own, surgery is the mainstay in most cases — home care and medicines play a supporting role.
fistula.treat.home.d: While you await treatment: warm sitz baths, pain relief such as paracetamol, and keeping the area clean — these support comfort but do not close a fistula on their own.
fistula.treat.med.d: Antibiotics only when a doctor directs them — for example, for an associated infection; antibiotics alone do not close a fistula.
fistula.treat.proc.d: Fistulotomy — the whole length of a simple fistula is laid open so it can heal into a flat scar; typically used when only a small amount of muscle is involved. Seton — a surgical thread is looped through the fistula and left in place to keep it draining and allow gradual healing; commonly used for fistulas involving more muscle, often before or instead of a further procedure.
fistula.treat.surg.d: Endorectal advancement flap — a flap of healthy tissue covers the internal opening, avoiding cutting the sphincter muscle; the LIFT procedure — the tunnel passing between the sphincter muscles is closed, usually after a seton stage. Complex fistulas may need treatment in stages, and fistulas linked to inflammatory bowel disease may also be managed with medicines under a specialist (for example, biologic therapy).
fistula.treat.out: Which operation suits you depends on the fistula's pathway and how much of the sphincter muscle it involves — your surgeon will examine you, discuss the options and their risks, and advise what is appropriate.
fistula.prevent.i1: There is no reliable way to prevent a fistula, but prompt treatment of an anal abscess lowers the chance of one forming
fistula.prevent.i2: If you have Crohn's disease or another inflammatory bowel condition, stay under specialist care
fistula.prevent.i3: Keep stools soft with fibre and fluids — pain medicines can cause constipation, so fibre supplements with plenty of water are often advised
fistula.prevent.i4: After surgery, take warm sitz baths and follow the wound-care and dressing instructions from the care team
fistula.prevent.i5: See a doctor without delay if signs of infection appear — fever, swelling or redness
fistula.recov.p: Most fistula procedures are day cases, though some people need an overnight stay or further staged operations. Recovery commonly takes several weeks and depends on how complex the fistula is. The wound heals from the inside out and may need dressings and time. Fistulas can come back after surgery, and there is a small risk of temporary or lasting effects on bowel control — your surgeon will discuss these. Keep all follow-up appointments so healing can be checked.
